Cuckoo chicks compete with host chicks by growing faster, being larger, being more aggressive (pushing host chicks aside for food), and mimicking host chicks' begging calls to trick hosts into feeding them.

Brood parasitism by cuckoos harms hosts: fewer host chicks fledge (population decline for the host species), and feeding a large cuckoo chick is energetically costly, reducing host survival and reproductive success. #cuckoo #brood_parasitism

Host birds detect cuckoo eggs by visual inspection (size, shape, color differ from their own eggs) and by remembering cuckoo egg appearance from past experience; some also use vocal recognition of cuckoo calls. #cuckoo #host_birds

Host species best at detecting/rejecting cuckoo eggs include the European magpie (particularly adept), reed warbler, dunnock, and meadow pipit. Effectiveness varies by host species and ecological conditions.

Cuckoo chick predators include birds of prey (hawks, owls, eagles), ground predators (foxes, cats), and other birds such as magpies and jays once outside the nest. Cuckoo chicks stay still and silent to avoid detection, and the larger number of birds in the nest offers some protection. #cuckoo

Host species best at detecting/rejecting cuckoo eggs include the European magpie (particularly adept), reed warbler, dunnock, and meadow pipit; effectiveness varies by host species and ecological conditions. #cuckoo #host_birds
